newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU set to appeal against WTO meat hormone ruling.
newsitem.headline: EU set to appeal against WTO meat hormone ruling.

text.p: The European Commission seemed certain on Tuesday to appeal against a World Trade Organisation (WTO) dispute panel ruling that its ban on imports of hormone-treated meat breaks free trade rules.

The Commission said in a statement the panel failed to take properly into account scientific evidence presented by the European Union in support of its ban, which mainly affects imports from the United States.

"They (the WTO panel) have ruled that no member...is allowed to establish its own level of protection. Our view is contrary to that," a Commission spokesman told a news briefing. "It's quite clear that there will be an appeal."
"The Commission considers that the matter must be brought before the appellate body of the WTO," the statement said.
Commission officials said a formal decision to appeal could only be taken after the 15 EU member states had been consulted.
Support is widely expected. France has said that it would ban imports of U.S. hormone-meat even if it incurred heavy fines.
Trade sources in Geneva said the panel's final ruling in favour of the United States, was delivered to EU and U.S. missions in Geneva on Monday.

Washington had been backed in its complaint by Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Norway. Argentina, which exports beef untreated with hormones to many EU member states, voiced support for the Brussels position.
The European Commission was also concerned about broader aspects of the WTO panel ruling, the Commission spokesman said.
Under WTO rules, each member has the right to establish what level of health protection is needed for its citizens. But the panel's report seemed to curb this right, he added.
"This finding has implications for everybody, including the United States," the spokesman said.

The EU has 41 days to appeal and this could be made in early August if there was a meeting scheduled of the WTO appeals committee, the spokesman estimated. The WTO would then have up to 90 days to issue a final ruling which would point to early November.

EU officials have indicated they see little prospect of lifting the restrictions, which were officially imposed for health reasons, because of strong consumer pressure against the sale of beef treated with hormones.

If the EU loses an appeal -- as is almost certain -- but still declines to act, the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) could askt the EU to pay compensation to the United States for the amount of trade it says it has lost.
If the EU refused, the DSB -- on which all the WTO's 131 members have a voice -- could authorise U.S. trade retaliation to the same amount.

In 1989, two years after first bringing the case to the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), the United States slapped 10 percent duties on a range of agricultural goods from the EU worth around $90 million a year.

In July last year the EU asked the DSB to set up a panel to look into the legality of the U.S. counter-action, but two weeks later Washington lifted the duties pending a decision in its case against Brussels.
